Why a CAA Record Blocks Certificate Issuance

"CAA record prevents issuance" (or "Blocking CAA record(s) found") is one of the most-repeated error messages on certbot's own GitHub issue tracker and Let's Encrypt's community support forum. It has four distinct causes, and fixing one does not fix the others — a domain can have more than one of these problems layered on top of each other, so work through all four before assuming the record is clean.

1. The record that actually applies isn't at the name you think it is

A certificate authority does not check only the exact hostname you're requesting a certificate for. Per RFC 8659's processing rules, if that name has no CAA records of its own, the CA walks up to its parent domain — then that domain's parent, and so on — until it finds a domain that publishes a CAA record set, or runs out of domain entirely. A restriction on example.com applies to staging.example.com, app.staging.example.com, and every other name under it, unless one of those subdomains publishes its own CAA record that overrides it.

This tool's "found at" line names the actual domain in the tree the applicable record set lives at — which is frequently a parent domain you weren't thinking about when a subdomain's renewal started failing.

2. The record exists and simply doesn't name your CA

If a CAA record set exists at the applicable name and lists one or more CAs, and the CA you're trying to use isn't one of them, that CA is required to refuse issuance. This is CAA working exactly as designed — the fix is adding an issue record naming the CA you actually want to use (by its own documented issuer domain, e.g. letsencrypt.org for Let's Encrypt or pki.goog for Google Trust Services), or removing the CAA record set entirely if you no longer need the restriction.

3. A disallow-all record

An issue record whose value is a lone semicolon — 0 issue ";" — explicitly authorizes no certificate authority at all for non-wildcard certificates. An issuewild record with the same value does the same specifically for wildcard certificates. Both are easy to introduce by mistake while hand-editing a zone file (a stray semicolon left over from a template, or a "block everything while we set this up properly" placeholder that never got removed), and the fix is simply deleting or replacing the record.

4. A critical, unrecognized property tag

RFC 8659 defines exactly three standard property tags: issue, issuewild, and iodef. A record can mark any tag — including a custom one, or a typo of a standard one — with the "critical" flag. When it does, a compliant CA that does not specifically implement that exact tag must refuse to issue for the domain at all, regardless of any issue records also present in the set. Since no public certificate authority implements an arbitrary custom tag, a critical flag on one effectively blocks every CA until the record is fixed — and it is invisible in a plain record listing that doesn't specifically apply this rule. This tool flags it explicitly rather than only showing the raw record text.

What this tool does and doesn't check

It reads the CAA record set your DNS publishes and applies the rules above — that is evidence about your DNS configuration, not a guarantee that a specific CA will actually issue. The CA still applies its own domain-validation, rate-limit, and account checks on top of CAA authorization.

Common questions

What is a CAA record, and why would it block my certificate?

A CAA (Certification Authority Authorization) DNS record names which certificate authorities are allowed to issue TLS certificates for your domain. If it names one CA and you (or your hosting provider) try to get a certificate from a different one, that CA is required to refuse — this is one of the most common causes of a sudden, confusing certificate-renewal failure, especially after switching hosts or CDNs.

Why check the parent domain, not just the exact hostname?

RFC 8659 says a certificate authority does not stop at the exact name you're requesting a certificate for. If app.staging.example.com has no CAA records of its own, the CA checks staging.example.com, then example.com, and uses whichever ancestor domain has the first non-empty answer. A tool that queries only the exact name reports "no CAA record, any CA may issue" for a subdomain whose parent actually restricts issuance. See how this compares to a plain DNS lookup.

What does a critical, unrecognized property tag actually do?

RFC 8659 defines exactly three standard tags (issue, issuewild, iodef). A record can mark any tag — including a custom or misspelled one — as "critical", and a compliant CA that does not specifically implement that tag must then refuse to issue for the domain at all, regardless of any issue records also present. Since no public CA implements an arbitrary custom tag, a critical flag on one effectively blocks every CA until the record is fixed — and it is invisible in a plain record listing that doesn't apply this rule.

Does a clean report guarantee my certificate will issue?

No. This reports what your published CAA records authorize, computed the way RFC 8659 says a CA must compute it — it is evidence about your DNS configuration, not a determination that a given CA will actually issue. The CA may apply its own additional checks (domain validation, rate limits, account restrictions) on top of CAA authorization.

Is it safe to point this at a hostname?

This tool never sends any request to the hostname you name — it only queries Cloudflare's public DNS-over-HTTPS resolver, reading CAA and CNAME records the domain owner already published for anyone to see. Nothing is uploaded to our servers when run in the browser; every request goes straight from your browser to the DNS resolver.

Evidence, not a determination. This reads the CAA record set your DNS actually publishes and reports what RFC 8659 says it authorizes. It is not a guarantee that any particular certificate authority will actually issue a certificate — the CA applies its own checks on top of CAA authorization, and this tool does not perform a full security or compliance audit.

CAA Record Checker vs. a Plain DNS Lookup

dig CAA yourdomain.com, or pasting a hostname into a generic online DNS-record viewer, is the first thing most people reach for when a certificate authority reports "CAA record prevents issuance." It's the right instinct, and it isn't wrong — it's incomplete, in a way that matters specifically for this record type.

What a plain lookup shows you

The raw CAA record text at exactly the name you queried. If that name genuinely has no CAA records, most plain lookup tools report "no CAA record found" and stop there — a perfectly correct answer to the question they asked, which is narrower than the question you actually have.

Why that isn't the whole answer

RFC 8659 ruleA plain lookupThis tool
Walk up to a parent domain when the exact name has no CAA recordReports "none found" and stopsWalks up automatically, names the ancestor it found the applicable record at
issuewild overrides issue for wildcard certsShows both records; you work out which appliesApplies the fallback rule and reports the wildcard verdict directly
A critical, unrecognized tag blocks every non-implementing CAShows the raw tag; easy to miss the implicationFlags it explicitly as a finding
Is a specific named CA actually authorized?You compare the record text to the CA's issuer domain by eyeNames the verdict directly for 8 known CAs, or any CA domain you enter

Common questions

What does a plain DNS lookup (dig CAA, or a generic online CAA viewer) show me?

The raw CAA record text at exactly the hostname you queried — nothing more. If that name has no records, most plain lookup tools report "no CAA record found" and stop there, even when a parent domain actually restricts issuance for it.

Why isn't that enough to know whether a certificate will be blocked?

Because RFC 8659 does not evaluate CAA at only the exact name. A certificate authority walks up the DNS tree to the first ancestor domain that publishes a CAA record set, applies the issuewild-overrides-issue fallback for wildcard certificates, and must refuse issuance entirely if any record carries the critical flag on a tag it doesn't recognize. A raw record dump tells you what's published; it doesn't tell you what those rules mean for a specific certificate authority you're trying to use.

Does this tool replace dig or a plain lookup?

No — both are useful, for different questions. A plain lookup answers "what CAA record is published at this exact name?" quickly, with no interpretation. This tool answers the question that actually matters when a certificate fails to issue: "which certificate authorities are authorized, once the real tree-walk and fallback rules are applied?" It is still the right tool for simply confirming a record you just added is visible. See why a CAA record blocks issuance for the full walkthrough of all four causes.
